source.title: Superposition Yields Robust Neural Scaling
source.authors: Yizhou Liu; Zi-Ming Liu; Jeff Gore

record.file_problem: none; full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper trains a modified toy superposition autoencoder and measures representation, overlap geometry, and loss across model widths, feature-frequency distributions, and weight-decay settings. It tests superposition-related behavior conceptually, rather than reproducing the original study’s full method.
record.gate_note: The paper also analyzes open-source LLM output-head vectors and evaluation losses; those results do not measure the neuron-spread or SAE-recovery behavior named in V4, so they are recorded under fits_no_version. Values used only to choose fitting ranges or hyperparameters are not rows.
record.test_reason: The study trains Anthropic's toy superposition autoencoder with an added weight-decay knob that controls the degree of superposition. Its results bear on V1: how many features get represented beyond m, and whether the overlap geometry is ETF-like or regular. Most of its headline results are loss-vs-width scaling exponents, which V1 does not name; those go to fits_no_version. It does not vary sparsity to locate a transition. It has no neuron-basis, polysemanticity or SAE analysis, and its LLM work measures only LM-head token-vector overlaps and losses.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors conclude that strong superposition yields robust inverse-width loss scaling via geometric interference in toy models. They claim open LLMs are in strong superposition with about 1/m overlaps and αm≈0.91, and that Chinchilla (αm≈0.88) is consistent. They name superposition a central driver of neural scaling laws. They acknowledge the toy model is not rigorously solved and that the reasons LLMs reach strong superposition were not studied.
record.recipe_differences: Uses Anthropic’s toy superposition autoencoder with minor modifications to data sampling and adds decoupled weight decay or growth to control superposition systematically; focuses on loss scaling with width.
record.method_sensitivity: Toy-model outcomes vary with weight decay, feature-frequency distribution and exponent, and activation density (which changes the loss coefficient but not the reported exponent).

fits_no_version.finding: In toy models, strong superposition gives loss scaling close to 1/m across exponential, power-law and linear frequency distributions (αm 0.89–1.01). Under weak superposition, loss is a power law only if feature frequencies are a power law, with αm≈α−1.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Superposition regime determines how representation-limited loss scales with width: about 1/m in the strong regime, and frequency-dependent in the weak regime.

fits_no_version.finding: LLM LM-head token-vector mean squared overlaps roughly follow 1/m, all rows have nonzero norm, and fitted evaluation-loss width exponent is 0.91±0.04.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: LLM unembedding vectors are in a strong-superposition-like regime with about 1/m squared overlaps, consistent with near-inverse-width loss scaling.

record.problems: The toy model is a simplified autoencoder, and the authors state they do not rigorously solve it. The LLM-to-token mapping is described as naive; LLM overlap data are noisy, and the paper does not establish that the measured representation loss is the causal source of observed LLM scaling. The authors also note that the ETF-based account is oversimplified for highly skewed feature frequencies.

untested.parts: A sparsity-dependent phase transition: superposition is controlled by weight decay, not by scanning sparsity, and represented fraction is not reported versus density. Small-n regular polytope geometry such as digons or pentagons. Whether naturally trained networks (γ=0) reach the same regimes.
Not tested. The hidden layer has no privileged neuron basis, so there is no polysemanticity analysis.
Not tested. The LLM analysis uses LM-head token-vector overlaps and row norms only.
Not tested. Features are scalar by construction, and there is no comparison with multi-dimensional features.

missing.what: Number of strongly represented features (norm>1) far exceeds m but is bounded near m²/2, matching the ETF bound. This is a capacity and geometry result for V1.
Mean squared overlap over all vectors in the strong regime sits above 1/m but scales as 1/m, even at large α.
More frequent features get larger norms and are more likely represented. Row norms are bimodal (near 0 and 1 under positive weight decay; around 1 under negative).
Large toy models (n=10240): ϕ1/2=1 in the strong regime versus about m/n in the weak regime, and mean squared overlap of strongly represented features is close to κ²≈1/m.

record.verdict_notes: Not an original source. Only rows on represented fraction and overlap geometry bear on V1; the scaling-exponent rows are the paper's own claim. Superposition here is partly imposed: γ<0 explicitly pushes rows to unit norm, so 'strong superposition' is induced, not purely emergent. Small weight decay also gives it, per Figure 3b.

versions.untested_parts: Does not establish that naturally trained networks enter the toy model’s regimes without the imposed weight-decay control. It does not test a general transition law across network architectures or feature structures beyond its toy autoencoder.
Does not test polysemantic neurons or whether important features receive dedicated neuron dimensions while other features share them.
Does not investigate alternative causes of polysemantic neurons.
The LLM analysis measures token-vector overlaps in the language-model head, not features spread across neurons or sparse features recovered by a dictionary or SAE.
Does not test whether SAE features are complete, stable, or canonical units.
The toy model represents each scalar feature with a row vector, but the paper does not compare one-dimensional features with multidimensional feature representations.

rows.baseline: Strong-superposition fits on the same distributions

rows.subject: toy model (small toy models)
rows.size_stated: data dimension n = 1000; model dimension m = 10, 15, 25, 39, 63, 100
rows.operation_detail: Measure normalized row-vector squared overlaps among strongly represented features.
rows.measure: Variance and mean of squared overlaps
rows.baseline: Random unit vectors have mean 1/m and variance m²(m−1) / [2(m+2)]; ETF variance is zero
rows.value: Strongly represented vectors are described as ETF-like; overlap variance can be near 0 for even feature frequencies, and mean squared overlap is 1/m
rows.note: The authors describe the measured geometry as ETF-like, not as an exact ETF.
rows.check: Linked correctly. Strongly represented vectors are ETF-like: overlap variance falls below the random-vector value (near 0 for small α), and mean squared overlap is about 1/m. This is regular geometry.

source_check.correct: Random unit vectors have squared-overlap mean 1/m and variance 2(m−1)/[m²(m+2)], asymptotically 2/m². The displayed baseline incorrectly rearranges the variance formula. The study identifies the squared-overlap distribution as Beta(1/2,(m−1)/2), which also determines this variance.
source_check.locator_found: Section 3.2, paragraph introducing the Beta distribution and Figure 5c–d; Appendix D.6.
source_check.problem: The random-vector variance formula in the baseline has its factors misplaced.

rows.subject: toy model (small toy models)
rows.size_stated: data dimension n = 1000; model dimension m = 10, 15, 25, 39, 63, 100
rows.operation_detail: Measure overlap geometry and width-scaling exponent as feature-frequency skew increases.
rows.measure: Overlap variance and loss model exponent αm
rows.baseline: Even-frequency strong-superposition case: αm near 1 and ETF-like overlap variance
rows.value: Overlap variance is larger for large α; αm increases with α and can deviate from 1. The paper reports αm close to 2(α − 1) in some cases, but says the real configuration is more complicated.
rows.uncertainty: Error bars are standard errors in Figure 5e; individual values not stated in text
rows.note: The authors say their ETF-based picture is oversimplified for highly skewed feature frequencies.
rows.check: Only the overlap-geometry part bears on V1. At large α the overlap variance grows and can exceed the random-vector value, so the geometry becomes less regular. The αm part is a scaling result.

source_check.locator_found: Section 3.2, Figure 5c,e; Appendix D.6, paragraphs discussing large α and overlap heterogeneity.

relationships.condition: Toy autoencoder (n=1000 and n=10240) with small or negative weight decay and relatively even feature frequencies
relationships.reason: ϕ1/2≈1≫m/n, so most features are represented in overlapping directions (R1). Strongly represented vectors are ETF-like, with variance below random and mean squared overlap about 1/m (R8).
relationships.display_finding: The represented fraction ϕ1/2 was about 1, far above m/n, so most features occupied overlapping directions. Strongly represented vectors were ETF-like, with overlap variance below random and mean squared overlap about 1/m.

relation.reason: Its own experiments measure represented-feature fractions and overlap geometry under controlled regularization and feature-frequency conditions.

tranche.reason: The modified toy autoencoder uses decoupled weight decay or growth to control superposition and measures representation coverage and overlap geometry, providing a different intervention bearing on V1.

source_check.notes: The study supports conditional overlapping storage and ETF-like geometry; it does not independently establish a sparsity-driven onset transition. The authors acknowledge that their geometric account does not rigorously solve the toy model.
